items.stem: Explain why log(MN) = log M + log N, using exponent laws.

items.answer: (a) M = 2ᵖ, N = 2^q (b) MN = 2^(p + q) so log₂(MN) = p + q (c) M/N = 2^(p − q) (d) e.g. M = 8, N = 2: log₂ 16 = 4 = 3 + 1
items.markingKey: (a) M = 2ᵖ, N = 2^q (b) MN = 2^(p + q) so log₂(MN) = p + q (c) M/N = 2^(p − q) (d) e.g. M = 8, N = 2: log₂ 16 = 4 = 3 + 1. Laws stated and applied (A1 M1); proof / verification (B: R1 A1); communication with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: Explain why log(M + N) is not equal to log M + log N.
items.answer: The product law turns multiplication into addition; there is no law for the log of a sum, e.g. log(10 + 10) = log 20 ≈ 1.30 but log 10 + log 10 = 2.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The product law turns multiplication into addition; there is no law for the log of a sum, e.g. log(10 + 10) = log 20 ≈ 1.30 but log 10 + log 10 = 2. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Before calculators, engineers in Dubai multiplied with slide rules, which add lengths proportional to logarithms. (a) Find log 5 and log 5. (b) Add them and show the result is log 25. (c) Explain how a slide rule multiplies. (d) Explain how it could divide 25 by 5.
items.answer: (a) log 5 ≈ 0.699, log 5 ≈ 0.699 (b) sum ≈ 1.40 = log 25 (c) multiplication becomes addition of lengths proportional to logs (d) subtract lengths: log(25) − log(5) = log 5

items.stem: Lars invests £2,000 in London at 6% per year compound interest. (a) Write an equation for when the investment reaches £3,000. (b) Solve it using logarithms. (c) State the number of whole years needed. (d) Explain why the answer is the same for any starting amount.
items.answer: (a) £2,000 × 1.06ᵗ = £3,000 (b) t = log 1.5/log 1.06 ≈ 6.96 (c) 7 whole years (d) the time does not depend on P

items.stem: A machine in a factory in Kuala Lumpur produces 75 dB. (a) Find its intensity using L = 10 log(I/10⁻¹²). (b) Find the level when 2 identical machines run together. (c) Compare with a safety limit of 85 dB. (d) Find the largest number of machines that can run together within the limit.
items.answer: (a) I = 10^(75/10) × 10⁻¹² = 0.0000316 W/m² (b) 2 machines: L = 75 + 10 log 2 ≈ 78.0 dB (c) within the 85 dB limit (d) the most machines allowed: 10

items.stem: Yusuf says a magnitude 7 earthquake is only "a bit stronger" than a magnitude 6. Explain why this is misleading.
items.answer: The Richter scale is logarithmic: a difference of 1 means 10¹ = 10 times the amplitude.
items.markingKey: Log scale (R1); factor (A1).

items.stem: Arjun says log₃ 27 = 27/3 = 9. Explain the mistake and give the correct value.
items.answer: A logarithm is an exponent, not a quotient: 3³ = 27, so log₃ 27 = 3.
items.markingKey: Meaning of log (R1); value (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "(log x)² = 2 log x." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The power law applies to log(x²), not to the square of the log.

items.stem: "If 4ˣ = 9, then x = 9/4." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: x = log 9 / log 4 ≈ 1.58.
items.markingKey: x = log 9 / log 4 ≈ 1.58. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo says a magnitude 7 earthquake is only "a bit stronger" than a magnitude 4. Explain why this is misleading.
items.answer: The Richter scale is logarithmic: a difference of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times the amplitude.
items.markingKey: Log scale (R1); factor (A1).

items.stem: Sana says log₂ 8 = 8/2 = 4. Explain the mistake and give the correct value.
items.answer: A logarithm is an exponent, not a quotient: 2³ = 8, so log₂ 8 = 3.

items.stem: A computer club in Melbourne wants to know how many digits 3³⁰ has. (a) Find log 10, log 100 and log 1000. (b) Explain the link between log N and the number of digits of N. (c) Find log(3³⁰) using log Nᵏ = k log N. (d) Hence state the number of digits.
items.answer: (a) log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3 (b) a whole number with d digits has d − 1 ≤ log N < d (c) log(3³⁰) = 30 log 3 ≈ 14.31 (d) 15 digits
items.markingKey: (a) log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3 (b) a whole number with d digits has d − 1 ≤ log N < d (c) log(3³⁰) = 30 log 3 ≈ 14.31 (d) 15 digits. Logarithms evaluated from the definition (A1 A1); pattern / link explained (B: R1 R1); communicated with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: Prove the logarithm laws for base 3. (a) Let log₃ M = p and log₃ N = q; write M and N as powers of 3. (b) Prove the product law. (c) Prove the quotient law. (d) Check the product law with a numerical example.
items.answer: (a) M = 3ᵖ, N = 3^q (b) MN = 3^(p + q) so log₃(MN) = p + q (c) M/N = 3^(p − q) (d) e.g. M = 27, N = 3: log₃ 81 = 4 = 3 + 1

items.stem: Seismologists in Melbourne recorded a magnitude 4.8 earthquake and later a magnitude 6.3 one. (a) Compare their amplitudes. (b) Energy grows as 10^(1.5M); compare their energies. (c) Find the magnitude of a quake with twice the amplitude of the first. (d) Explain why a logarithmic scale is used.
items.answer: (a) 31.6 times the amplitude (b) energy ratio ≈ 10^(1.5 × 1.5) ≈ 178 (c) M = 4.8 + log 2 ≈ 5.10 (d) a linear scale would need numbers from 1 to about 10⁹
